lineage_note: Lineages are the field's own claims grouped for the rail: what it is: a routing layer for AI tasks (F1, F2, F3, F18); what is available and what is planned (F4, F5, F8, F9, F13, F43, F44, F46); evidence: benchmark observations and the Pareto frontier (F6, F7, F11); task families and their contracts (F10, F12, F14, F15); evidence: its stated limits (F16, F17, F39, F40, F42, F68); maker and editor (F19, F20, F57, F65, F67, F69); independence and paid work (F21, F37, F63); how it holds the name (F22); Papers with Code as it records it: the end (F23, F28, F32, F48, F50); the successor to Papers with Code (F24, F26, F27, F38, F47, F49, F56, F58, F64, F71); Papers with Code as it records it: what it was (F25, F29, F30); where Papers with Code's data went (F31, F51); no single replacement (F33, F52); the record's rules: code, dates, corrections (F34, F35, F36, F62); data access and licence (F41, F53, F70); the class it refuses: aggregator (F45, F66); what it is: a registry of benchmarks (F54, F55, F61); the unit: the benchmark row (F59, F60). Three self-presentations stand in the field at three addresses, each its own lineage: a routing layer for AI tasks (B1), the successor to Papers with Code (B2, B3, B4) and a registry of benchmarks (B4); the field relates them itself at F43 ('the registry is routable'), and at F45 and F66 it refuses the class aggregator.

F1.quote: CodeSOTA — One Routing Layer for AI Tasks
F1.claim: what it is, by its title: one routing layer for AI tasks
F1.lineage: what it is: a routing layer for AI tasks

F2.quote: One routing layer for AI tasks. Compare models for documents, code, speech, and vision, inspect benchmark evidence, and explore the CodeSOTA selection and execution API.
F2.claim: one routing layer: compare models for documents, code, speech and vision; inspect evidence; a selection and execution API
F2.lineage: what it is: a routing layer for AI tasks

F3.quote: Start with the work you need done. Compare models across quality and cost, inspect the evidence, and use a common API to choose a route.
F3.claim: the method: start from the work, compare on quality and cost, inspect evidence, choose a route through a common API
F3.lineage: what it is: a routing layer for AI tasks

F4.quote: Available today: model selection across the registry and an execution API for code & text. Document, speech, and vision execution are planned.
F4.claim: available today: model selection across the registry and execution for code and text; document, speech and vision execution planned
F4.lineage: what is available and what is planned

F5.quote: This preview returns model recommendations. It does not process your files or run inference.
F5.claim: the preview recommends models; it does not process files or run inference
F5.lineage: what is available and what is planned

F6.quote: Choose a task, compare actual benchmark observations, and inspect the Pareto frontier before selecting a route.
F6.claim: choose a task, compare benchmark observations, inspect the Pareto frontier, then select a route
F6.lineage: evidence: benchmark observations and the Pareto frontier

F7.quote: Every dot is a recorded result. Highlighted models have no competitor in this cohort that is at least as good on both axes and strictly better on one.
F7.claim: the Pareto frontier defined: each dot a recorded result; highlighted models undominated in the cohort
F7.lineage: evidence: benchmark observations and the Pareto frontier

F8.quote: Our direction is a common API and account across AI tasks, with versioned recipes and a stable output contract for each task.
F8.claim: its direction (stated as such): a common API and account across tasks, versioned recipes, a stable output contract per task
F8.lineage: what is available and what is planned

F9.locus: 'The product we are building', third note
F9.quote: The roadmap brings provider adapters, versioned recipes, task validation, fallback, and usage accounting into the same routing layer.
F9.claim: on the roadmap: provider adapters, versioned recipes, task validation, fallback and usage accounting
F9.lineage: what is available and what is planned

F10.locus: 'The product we are building', first note
F10.quote: Each task keeps its own output format across providers.
F10.claim: a contract per task: each task keeps its own output format across providers

F11.locus: 'The product we are building', second note
F11.quote: Compare models on the same task and protocol, with measured quality, latency, and cost as coverage grows.
F11.claim: evidence behind each route: same task and protocol, measured quality, latency and cost, as coverage grows
F11.lineage: evidence: benchmark observations and the Pareto frontier

F12.quote: Turn scans and PDFs into text, tables, or structured fields. Choose for your documents, language, and deployment.
F12.claim: documents, the next execution family: scans and PDFs into text, tables or fields

F13.quote: Explore the task guides and evidence behind future speech routes and the existing coding API.
F13.claim: speech routes are future; the coding API exists
F13.lineage: what is available and what is planned

F14.quote: Transcribe recordings or generate a voice. Compare language coverage, latency, intelligibility, and deployment.
F14.claim: speech: transcription and voice generation, compared on coverage, latency, intelligibility, deployment

F15.quote: Generate functions or repair a repository. Compare models and agents on evidence that matches the work.
F15.claim: coding: generation and repository repair, models and agents compared on matching evidence

F16.quote: A strong result on one test does not guarantee a fit for your documents, recordings, or repository.
F16.claim: a stated limit: a strong result on one test does not guarantee fit

F17.quote: Distinguish reported results from independently reproduced runs.
F17.claim: reported results kept apart from independently reproduced runs

F18.quote: CodeSOTA helps developers choose AI tools for documents, speech, and coding, with practical comparisons and inspectable benchmark evidence.
F18.claim: what it is, in its footer: it helps developers choose AI tools for documents, speech and coding
F18.lineage: what it is: a routing layer for AI tasks

F19.claim: its maker, in the header: 'By Fabryka AI'

F20.quote: © 2026 Codesota·Built by Kacper Wikiel in Warsaw
F20.claim: built by Kacper Wikiel in Warsaw

F21.quote: Built in public from Warsaw · open JSON · rankings stay earned
F21.claim: built in public, open JSON, rankings earned

F22.claim: the homepage names Papers with Code once, as a footer link

F23.quote: Papers With Code was retired by Meta in July 2025.
F23.claim: Papers with Code retired by Meta in July 2025
F23.lineage: Papers with Code as it records it: the end

F24.quote: Use CodeSOTA for maintained SOTA leaderboards, benchmark pages, API replacement notes, and links to the frozen paperswithcode-data archive.
F24.claim: use CodeSOTA for maintained SOTA leaderboards, benchmark pages, API notes and links to the frozen archive
F24.lineage: the successor to Papers with Code

F25.quote: Papers with Code was, in effect, the Wikipedia of machine-learning research: a wiki of papers linked to implementations, benchmarks organised as <Task, Dataset, Metric> tuples, and leaderboards that showed, for each tuple, who currently held the top score and with what code.
F25.claim: Papers with Code, as it describes it: the Wikipedia of ML research, papers linked to code, benchmarks as Task–Dataset–Metric tuples, leaderboards
F25.lineage: Papers with Code as it records it: what it was

F26.quote: This page is our record of what happened, what was lost, and where to look now — with Codesota positioned as the calmer, stricter successor.
F26.claim: the page is its record of Papers with Code's end, with Codesota positioned as the calmer, stricter successor
F26.lineage: the successor to Papers with Code

F27.lineage: the successor to Papers with Code

F28.quote: On July 24–25, 2025, Meta sunsetted Papers with Code without prior notice.
F28.claim: Meta sunsetted Papers with Code on 24–25 July 2025 without notice
F28.lineage: Papers with Code as it records it: the end

F29.quote: the 9,327 benchmark leaderboards, 79,817 paper-to-code linkages and 5,628 datasets that had been tracked were no longer served from the canonical URL.
F29.claim: 9,327 leaderboards, 79,817 paper–code links and 5,628 datasets no longer served
F29.lineage: Papers with Code as it records it: what it was

F30.quote: The site had been acquired by Meta (then Facebook AI) in December 2019 from its founders Robert Stojnic and Ross Taylor, under a public commitment that it would “remain a neutral, open and free resource.”
F30.claim: acquired by Meta (then Facebook AI) in December 2019 from Stojnic and Taylor, under a commitment to remain neutral, open and free
F30.lineage: Papers with Code as it records it: what it was

F31.quote: Historical data was rescued by the community — as JSON dumps on GitHub, as the pwc-archive on Hugging Face, and as 2021-era imports into the Open Research Knowledge Graph. The data survives; the integrated experience does not.
F31.claim: the data rescued as JSON dumps, the pwc-archive and ORKG imports; the data survives, the integrated experience does not
F31.lineage: where Papers with Code's data went

F32.quote: The domain now redirects to Hugging Face Trending Papers; the leaderboards are gone.
F32.claim: the domain redirects to Hugging Face Trending Papers; the leaderboards are gone
F32.lineage: Papers with Code as it records it: the end

F33.quote: None of the successors Meta pointed at — Hugging Face Trending Papers, Semantic Scholar, Connected Papers — replicate the unified paper-code-benchmark-dataset-method linkage.
F33.claim: no successor Meta pointed at replicates the unified linkage

F34.quote: Five qualities of PWC at its best, carried forward into Codesota by default rather than by aspiration.
F34.claim: five qualities of PWC carried forward by default
F34.lineage: the record's rules: code, dates, corrections

F35.quote: Every submission carries code — a frozen commit, a declared environment, a recorded seed. If it does not run, the row does not publish.
F35.claim: every submission carries code; if it does not run, the row does not publish
F35.lineage: the record's rules: code, dates, corrections

F36.quote: Every score is stamped with the day it was published and the day it was verified.
F36.claim: every score stamped with publication and verification dates
F36.lineage: the record's rules: code, dates, corrections

F37.quote: Maintained independently, not owned by any single model vendor. Sponsored evaluations, when they exist, are flagged as such.
F37.claim: maintained independently, not vendor-owned; sponsored evaluations flagged

F38.quote: Codesota is the v2 replacement for what PWC did — reproduced scores with verification dates, code links, and lineage.
F38.claim: Codesota as the v2 replacement for what PWC did
F38.lineage: the successor to Papers with Code

F39.quote: Third-party sources listed for coverage — we do not claim their numbers were independently reproduced.
F39.claim: a stated limit: third-party sources' numbers not claimed as reproduced

F40.quote: “Reproduced” here means an independently executed run or a signed container hash — not an aggregated claim.
F40.claim: 'reproduced' defined: an independent run or a signed container hash

F41.quote: Historical PWC data | JSON dump, frozen | /browse/pwc
F41.claim: historical PWC data, a frozen JSON dump, at /browse/pwc

F42.quote: What never publishes is a number with no source.

F43.quote: Third, the registry is routable. Every benchmark row corresponds to an API endpoint; we are slowly building the “router” that lets a caller send a prompt or a document to the current SOTA without rewriting their code when the SOTA changes.
F43.claim: the registry is routable: each row an endpoint; the router being built on it
F43.lineage: what is available and what is planned

F44.quote: Everything else — the wiki-style task pages, the dataset cards, the method explanations — we are rebuilding gradually, in the open, one modality at a time.
F44.claim: task pages, dataset cards and method explanations rebuilt gradually
F44.lineage: what is available and what is planned

F45.quote: Unlike aggregator sites, CodeSOTA verifies results independently and focuses on practical recommendations for production use.
F45.claim: not an aggregator site: it verifies results independently

F46.quote: CodeSOTA is building comprehensive ML benchmarks starting with OCR and document AI.
F46.claim: building comprehensive ML benchmarks, starting with OCR and document AI
F46.lineage: what is available and what is planned

F47.quote: CodeSOTA is rebuilding this infrastructure independently.
F47.claim: rebuilding Papers with Code's infrastructure independently
F47.lineage: the successor to Papers with Code

F48.quote: Meta retired Papers with Code in July 2025, with the public shutdown observed around July 24-25, 2025.
F48.claim: Meta retired Papers with Code in July 2025, the shutdown observed 24–25 July
F48.lineage: Papers with Code as it records it: the end

F49.locus: 'At a glance', Where to start now
F49.quote: Archive for history; CodeSOTA for live SOTA
F49.claim: where to start: the archive for history, CodeSOTA for live SOTA
F49.lineage: the successor to Papers with Code

F50.quote: Users looking for paperswithcode.com were pushed toward Hugging Face, while the comprehensive task-based SOTA tracker and public API were no longer maintained.
F50.claim: users pushed toward Hugging Face; the SOTA tracker and API no longer maintained
F50.lineage: Papers with Code as it records it: the end

F51.quote: Historical dumps remain useful for reconstruction, citation checks, and migration work, but they should not be treated as a current leaderboard.
F51.claim: the dumps are useful for history, not a current leaderboard
F51.lineage: where Papers with Code's data went

F52.quote: There is no single drop-in replacement. Pick by job: historical archive, paper metadata, discovery feed, human benchmark browsing, or machine-readable SOTA lookup.
F52.claim: no single drop-in replacement; pick by job

F53.quote: Programmatic current-SOTA lookup for agents and internal tools.

F54.quote: Codesota is an independent registry of machine-learning benchmarks, maintained by Kacper Wikiel in Warsaw.
F54.claim: what it is, on its about page: an independent registry of ML benchmarks, maintained by Kacper Wikiel in Warsaw
F54.lineage: what it is: a registry of benchmarks

F55.quote: Codesota is an open, dated record of machine-learning benchmarks. It is maintained by one person, in public, with a clear separation between paid vendor work and public ranking integrity.
F55.claim: an open, dated record of ML benchmarks, maintained by one person, paid work kept apart from ranking
F55.lineage: what it is: a registry of benchmarks

F56.quote: Started 10 December 2025 after Meta retired Papers with Code. The goal is a calmer, stricter record — one that survives its authors.
F56.claim: started 10 December 2025 after Meta retired Papers with Code; the goal a record that survives its authors
F56.lineage: the successor to Papers with Code

F58.quote: Codesota is the attempt to rebuild that infrastructure in a way that cannot be retired by a press release.
F58.claim: the attempt to rebuild the infrastructure so that it cannot be retired by a press release
F58.lineage: the successor to Papers with Code

F59.quote: It is, plainly, a website and a JSON file. Each benchmark is a task-dataset-metric triple with a declared direction, a fixed split, a reproducibility package and a dated submission.
F59.claim: the unit: a benchmark as a task–dataset–metric triple, with direction, split, reproducibility package and dated submission

F60.quote: Each row carries a verification tier — self-reported, community-reproduced, or Codesota-reproduced — and each score is stamped with the day it was run.
F60.claim: verification tiers per row; each score dated

F61.quote: The philosophical commitment is modest: a registry, not a leaderboard. A leaderboard is a view of “who is on top right now”; a registry is the record that makes that view legible.
F61.claim: a registry, not a leaderboard, the two defined
F61.lineage: what it is: a registry of benchmarks

F62.quote: When a score turns out to be wrong, the correction is visible too. Nothing is silently deleted.
F62.lineage: the record's rules: code, dates, corrections

F63.quote: Vendors can pay for custom benchmarks, commissioned evaluations, profile pages, and publication support, but that work is disclosed inline where it appears. The public ranking method is not for sale.
F63.claim: paid vendor work disclosed inline; the ranking method not for sale

F64.quote: Meta shut Papers with Code in July 2025. Codesota launched on 10 December 2025 as an explicit successor attempt.
F64.claim: launched 10 December 2025 as an explicit successor attempt
F64.lineage: the successor to Papers with Code

F65.quote: Codesota is not a company raising a round. It has no investors, no board, no growth targets.
F65.claim: not a startup: no investors, board or growth targets

F66.quote: A new model announcement does not automatically become a row. A score becomes a row when it has a reproduction path and a dated submission — until then it is, at most, a claim.
F66.claim: not a press-release aggregator: a score is a row only with a reproduction path and dated submission

F67.quote: There is one editor. Submissions do not go through a review panel; they go through a reproduction run.
F67.claim: one editor; submissions go through a reproduction run, not a panel

F68.quote: The registry is a record of results; the primary literature is still the primary literature. Every row links back to its source, and the source is what you cite.
F68.claim: not a replacement for the paper: each row links to its source, which is what is cited

F69.quote: Codesota is written and maintained by Kacper Wikiel, in Warsaw. The repository, the registry and the site are one codebase, public on GitHub.
F69.claim: written and maintained by Kacper Wikiel in Warsaw; one public codebase

F70.quote: Registry data is published under CC BY 4.0. Cite codesota.com with the snapshot date; the JSON at /data/benchmarks.json is the canonical form.
F70.claim: registry data under CC BY 4.0; the JSON the canonical form

F71.claim: the dispatch dates itself, in its metadata, 25 July 2025 (modified 2026-04-22; its masthead reads 'Issue: April 22, 2026')
F71.lineage: the successor to Papers with Code
